name: Multilingual LibriSpeech (MLS)
description: A large-scale multilingual corpus suitable for speech research, derived from read audiobooks from LibriVox and consisting of 8 languages, including about 44.5K hours of English and about 6K hours for other languages.
creator: Vineel Pratap, Qiantong Xu, Anuroop Sriram, Gabriel Synnaeve, Ronan Collobert
inLanguage: English, German, Dutch, Spanish, French, Portuguese, Italian, Polish
citeAs: Vineel Pratap, Qiantong Xu, Anuroop Sriram, Gabriel Synnaeve, Ronan Collobert. MLS: A Large-Scale Multilingual Dataset for Speech Research. Preprint, December 22, 2020.
rai:dataCollection: The dataset was created from LibriVox read audiobooks and corresponding text sources. Audiobooks were downloaded for 8 selected languages based on audiobook hours and availability of corresponding text. Audio was downsampled, segmented into 10-20 second segments using trained acoustic models, pseudo labels were generated, source texts were downloaded or manually retrieved from online sources, normalized, and matched to pseudo labels to retrieve transcripts. Development and test transcripts were further human-verified by transcribers who corrected clear and obvious errors while listening to the audio.
rai:dataCollectionType: Web API, Web Scraping, Manual Human Curator, Software Collection, Document analysis
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Raw data consists of read audiobook audio from LibriVox and source text from audiobook text sources, mostly based on Project Gutenberg text data; for English, major text domains included gutenberg.org, archive.org, ccel.org and hathitrust.org. For some other languages, text was copied from browsers, extracted from PDF/EPUB books using pdftotext, or retrieved with HTML parsers.
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Audio files were segmented into 10-20 second segments by running acoustic model inference to generate Viterbi token sequences with timestamps, then splitting at the longest silence between 10 and 20 seconds or at 20 seconds if no silence was found. Source text was split into overlapping 1250-word documents with stride 1000 words. Candidate transcripts were retrieved using TF-IDF similarity on bigrams and Smith-Waterman alignment. Candidate transcripts were filtered out if WER between candidate transcript and pseudo label was greater than 40%. Numbers in matched text were replaced with aligned words from pseudo labels, and heuristics were used to handle hyphens and apostrophes.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Audio data was downsampled from 48kHz to 16kHz. Text normalization included NFKC normalization, removal of unwanted characters such as punctuation, subscript/superscripts, emojis, and escape symbols, removal of end-of-line hyphenation and joining split words, and filtering characters outside a valid unicode character list based on each language's orthography. Books with corrupted metadata, missing title, missing speaker/author information, multiple speakers, or duplicate versions were removed when creating splits.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Pseudo labels for segmented audio were generated by beam-search decoding with a 4-gram language model on acoustic models. Final transcripts were retrieved by matching pseudo labels to source book text using TF-IDF retrieval and Smith-Waterman alignment. For high-quality development and test sets, human transcribers listened to the audio while viewing the transcript and corrected mistakes, but were instructed to correct only clear and obvious errors.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Candidate transcripts were filtered if the WER between the candidate transcript and pseudo label was greater than 40%. For development and test sets, transcript quality was assessed by measuring WER between generated transcripts and human rated transcripts, reported per language.
rai:machineAnnotationTools: Trained acoustic models using Time-Depth Separable Convolutions with ASG loss; wav2letter@anywhere for streaming inference; beam-search decoding with a 4-gram language model; TF-IDF similarity on bigrams; Smith-Waterman alignment; pdftotext; num2words mentioned as a library considered for number conversion; SVM gender classifier with RBF kernel for speaker gender labeling
rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The dataset, language model training data, pre-built language models, pretrained models, and training recipes will be made freely available, but no update schedule, maintainer plan, or deprecation policy is specified.
rai:personalSensitiveInformation: Speaker gender was labeled with a gender classifier and used to balance development and test sets.
rai:dataSocialImpact: The authors state that the dataset will promote open research in large-scale training of ASR systems and multilingual ASR, and can also be used for Text-to-Speech research by extending LibriTTS to a larger multilingual version.
rai:dataBiases: To avoid potential bias from human transcribing, transcribers were instructed to correct only clear and obvious errors. Development and test sets were balanced in gender and duration. The source data is read speech from audiobooks, which may bias the dataset toward that speaking style.
rai:dataLimitations: Training data is lower than available audiobook data because text sources may not have been downloaded, candidate labels may have been filtered during transcript retrieval, or data may have been filtered while creating validation/test splits. Automatically extracting text for non-English audiobooks was challenging due to diverse domains and invalid links. The number replacement solution using pseudo labels is not perfect because pseudo labels may not always have the correct transcription. Polish language model decoding was negatively impacted by a 13% OOV rate. The dataset is based on read speech audiobooks.
rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is suitable for speech research, especially Automatic Speech Recognition and Text-to-Speech research. It provides train, development, and test splits, as well as limited supervision subsets including 10 hour, 1 hour, and six 10-minute training sets for low-resource training benchmarks. Development and test sets are intended for evaluation, and language models and baseline ASR models are also released.
